formula: estimate = starting premium × index(new) ÷ index(start), where index = driver and area factors × (liability share × limits × vehicle liability + damage share × deductible × loan or lease × vehicle age × vehicle damage)
changelogNote: Factors now come from public sources where we could find them: state insurance-department price surveys from Oklahoma, North Dakota, the District of Columbia, Texas, California, and Colorado; North Carolina's accident surcharge rule; NAIC and ISO premium and claim figures; and HLDI insurance losses by make and model. Everything else is labeled as our estimate and widens the range. The separate teen switch is gone; the 16–18 age band is the teen factor. Vehicle liability results are passed on only partly, the way insurers' vehicle ratings do.

driver-age.title: Driver age
driver-age.note: The main driver's age. 16–18 is the teen factor; there is no separate teen switch.

16-18.derivation: Texas 2025 (HelpInsure sample rates, liability only), age 18 ÷ age 30, single, same company, ZIP, car, use, and credit; male and female; +159% (median ratio 2.591; middle half of companies +135% to +241%) over 360 comparisons. Times the 26–39 factor above, because 30 is in that band. The site shows ages as bands (16–24, 25–64, 65+); TDI's data call rates them at 18, 30, and 65. The teen is the only driver on their own policy; adding a teen to a parent's policy is priced differently. For comparison, Oklahoma 2026's 16-year-old ÷ 55-year-old (who also differ in marital status, use, and mileage) is +351% (median ratio 4.507; middle half of companies +221% to +441%) over 200 comparisons.

16-18-added.label: 16–18, added to a parent's policy (whole household)
16-18-added.derivation: How much the whole household's policy goes up when a teen is added. California 2026, profile 2565 (married couple licensed 28 and 25 years, plus a 17-year-old licensed 1 year who "drives pleasure use only"; Camry 20,000 miles and Highlander 12,000 miles) ÷ profile 2555 (married couple licensed 13 and 10 years; Camry and Sienna, 15,000 miles each), with and without a multi-policy discount, same company and place: +51% (median ratio 1.511; middle half of companies +30% to +77%), 235 comparisons. That understates the teen, because the teen family's parents are more experienced and so cheaper. California's single drivers licensed 25 years ÷ 13 years (same company, place, car, and record) cost 9% less (median ratio 0.908; middle half of companies 13% less to 6% less), 247 comparisons, so we divide by that: +66%. This assumes the parents' experience credit works like a single driver's; it may be smaller on a two-driver policy, which would make the true figure lower, so the low edge goes down to the unadjusted figure. The second car and mileage also differ, and both are two-car households. It's the whole household's premium, not the teen's share, and it isn't a price for a teen's own car.

19-21.derivation: Oklahoma 2026, Scenario B (age 21, single) ÷ Scenario D (age 55, married); same commute, mileage, car, and coverage. Same company, city, and sex; +92% (median ratio 1.918; middle half of companies +69% to +106%) over 200 comparisons. Rough because marital status also differs.

22-25.derivation: District of Columbia 2024, age 25 ÷ age 39 (same company, same group: married, single female, single male; state-minimum coverage), +17% (median ratio 1.170; middle half of companies +10% to +31%) over 87 comparisons, times the 26–39 factor above (age 39 is in that band).

26-39.derivation: Oklahoma 2026, Scenario C (age 36) ÷ Scenario D (age 55): both married, 18-mile round-trip commute, 12,000 miles, same car and coverage. Same company, city, and sex; +11% (median ratio 1.109; middle half of companies +6% to +20%) over 200 comparisons.

65+.derivation: Median of two senior-versus-adult comparisons, times the 26–39 factor above (both adult ages are in that band). District of Columbia 2024, age 66 ÷ age 39 (same company and group; state-minimum coverage): 6% less (median ratio 0.939; middle half of companies 16% less to +3%), 87 comparisons. Texas 2025, age 65 ÷ age 30 (single male, and married): 5% less (median ratio 0.950; middle half of companies 10% less to no change), 360 comparisons.

driving-experience.title: Years licensed
driving-experience.note: Only used from age 26. For younger drivers the age factor already covers being new.

10+.label: Licensed 10 or more years
10+.derivation: The starting point for years licensed.

1-3.label: Licensed 1–3 years (age 26 and up)
1-3.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. California 2026 (licensed 2 years ÷ 13 years, liability only): +127% (median ratio 2.271; middle half of companies +84% to +173%), 103 comparisons. But California does not allow age as a rating factor (10 CCR §2632.5), so its newly licensed drivers are mostly young, and its years-licensed figure includes the youth effect our age factor already counts. We treat it as an upper bound, capped at the 19–21 age factor ÷ the 26–39 age factor (1.73), so an experienced-age driver never costs more than a young one. We don't know how much of the gap is experience and how much is age, so we take the middle of 1.00 and that upper bound on a multiplying scale (the square root). The range runs from 1.00 to the upper bound.

4-9.label: Licensed 4–9 years (age 26 and up)
4-9.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. California 2026 (licensed 4 and 7 years ÷ 13 years, liability-only and full-coverage profiles): +34% (median ratio 1.340; middle half of companies +24% to +55%), 494 comparisons. But California does not allow age as a rating factor (10 CCR §2632.5), so its newly licensed drivers are mostly young, and its years-licensed figure includes the youth effect our age factor already counts. We treat it as an upper bound, capped at the 19–21 age factor ÷ the 26–39 age factor (1.73), so an experienced-age driver never costs more than a young one. We don't know how much of the gap is experience and how much is age, so we take the middle of 1.00 and that upper bound on a multiplying scale (the square root). The range runs from 1.00 to the upper bound.

under-1.label: Licensed under 1 year (age 26 and up)
under-1.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. No survey we found prices a driver licensed under a year, and California, which does not allow age as a rating factor (10 CCR §2632.5), only goes down to 2 years. We use the 1–3 year estimate and raise the top of the range by a fifth, capped at the 16–18 age factor ÷ the 26–39 age factor (2.59).

not-used.label: Not used under 26
not-used.derivation: For drivers under 26 the age factor already covers being a new driver, so years licensed is not counted again.

driving-record.title: Driving record
driving-record.note: At-fault accidents in the last three years.

clean.label: Clean
clean.derivation: The starting point for driving record.

one.label: One at-fault accident
one.derivation: Median of three states. California 2026, one at-fault accident ÷ clean, same company, place, car, and years licensed (single-driver profiles, liability-only and full coverage): +41% (median ratio 1.411; middle half of companies +27% to +54%), 1091 comparisons; CDI says its survey premiums are "before any applicable discounts are applied", and company footnotes list California's Good Driver discount as one of those discounts (for example "California Good Driver Discount 30%" and "20% Good Driver Discount"). So the clean figures leave that discount out, and a California driver who loses it after an accident probably sees a bigger jump than this. Texas 2025, one at-fault accident ÷ clean (liability only): +52% (median ratio 1.521; middle half of companies +38% to +66%), 180 comparisons. North Carolina's Safe Driver Incentive Plan, set by state law: 40% for a small accident, 55% for a medium one, and 70% for $3,850 or more of damage or an injury; we count it as a median of 70% (typical claims are above $3,850) with 40% as the low edge.

two-or-more.label: Two or more at-fault accidents
two-or-more.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. Two North Carolina 3-point accidents would total 6 points; the NC page does not list the surcharge for 6 points, so we added two single-accident surcharges (1 + 0.70 + 0.70). The low end is one accident; the high end is the largest surcharge on the NC table (12 points, +340%).

7500-15000.label: 7,500–15,000 miles a year
7500-15000.derivation: The starting point for yearly mileage.

under-7500.label: Under 7,500 miles a year
under-7500.derivation: California 2026, 5,000–7,500 miles ÷ 7,600–10,000 miles, same company, car, record, and years licensed, Los Angeles: 8% less (median ratio 0.924; middle half of companies 12% less to 6% less), 360 comparisons.

over-15000.label: Over 15,000 miles a year
over-15000.derivation: Median of two rough comparisons. California 2026, 12,500–16,000 miles ÷ 7,600–10,000 miles, Los Angeles: +17% (median ratio 1.168; middle half of companies +9% to +21%), 360 comparisons (only part of that band is over 15,000). Texas 2025, commuting 18,000 miles ÷ pleasure use 10,000 miles: no change (median ratio 1.000; middle half of companies no change to +8%), 180 comparisons (use changes too).

no.label: No good-student discount
no.derivation: The starting point for good student.

yes.label: Good-student discount (under 26)
yes.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. Many insurers offer a discount for a B average or better.

no.label: No driver-training discount
no.derivation: The starting point for driver training.

yes.label: Driver-training discount (under 22)
yes.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. Many insurers offer a discount for completing driver education.

multi-policy.title: Bundling
multi-policy.note: Home or renters policy with the same company.

yes.label: Bundled with a home or renters policy
yes.derivation: California 2026, the same married household with and without a multi-policy discount (profiles 2555, 2565, 2592; full coverage), same company and place: 10% less (median ratio 0.900; middle half of companies 15% less to no change), 353 comparisons.

area.title: Area
area.note: Where the car is kept. Rural is the starting point.

urban.label: Urban
urban.derivation: Same company and driver, city versus rural area, in five states. Oklahoma 2026, Oklahoma City and Tulsa ÷ Woodward and McAlester: +16% (median ratio 1.163; middle half of companies +8% to +27%), 800 comparisons. North Dakota 2026, Fargo ÷ "Remainder of State" (Examples 1–3, 5–12): 1% less (median ratio 0.987; middle half of companies 11% less to +7%), 228. Texas 2025, Houston and Dallas ÷ Plainview and Alpine: +101% (median ratio 2.014; middle half of companies +75% to +138%), 2132. California 2026, Los Angeles Central ÷ Alturas: +66% (median ratio 1.659; middle half of companies +44% to +91%), 2583. Colorado 2023, Denver and Colorado Springs ÷ Sterling, Alamosa, and Craig: +29% (median ratio 1.286; middle half of companies +12% to +44%), 4344. The value is the middle of the five state medians. The states disagree a lot, so the low and high edges are the lowest and highest state medians (1% less to +101%), not the spread between companies.

suburban.label: Suburban
suburban.derivation: Rough. Only Texas, California, and Colorado publish a suburb, a city, and a rural area. Direct suburb ÷ rural, same company and driver: Texas 2025, Plano ÷ Plainview and Alpine: +65% (median ratio 1.653; middle half of companies +46% to +92%), 1066 comparisons. California 2026, Irvine ÷ Alturas: +31% (median ratio 1.307; middle half of companies +18% to +53%), 2582. Colorado 2023, Highlands Ranch ÷ Sterling, Alamosa, and Craig: +7% (median ratio 1.071; middle half of companies 3% less to +20%), 2172. The middle of those three is +31%, which is above our five-state urban factor (+29%), because these three states have bigger city-versus-rural gaps than the others. Multiplying suburb ÷ city in the same three states (17% less) by the urban factor gives +7%. We use neither. We measure where each state's suburb sits between its rural area and its city on a multiplying scale (Texas 0.72, California 0.53, Colorado 0.27 of the way), take the middle (0.53), and apply it to the urban factor: +14%. The low and high edges are the lowest and highest direct suburb ÷ rural figures.

rural.label: Rural
rural.derivation: The starting point for area. Other areas are compared with it.

liability-limits.title: Liability limits
liability-limits.note: How much the policy pays others. Moves only the liability share.

100-300-100.label: 100/300/100 limits
100-300-100.derivation: The starting point for liability limits.

state-minimum.label: State-minimum liability limits
state-minimum.derivation: Texas 2025, 30/60/25 (the Texas minimum) ÷ 100/300/100, liability only, same company, ZIP, and driver: 13% less (median ratio 0.870; middle half of companies 21% less to 10% less), 165 comparisons. Minimums differ by state, so the real difference in your state may be bigger or smaller.

250-500-250.label: Higher limits (250/500/250)
250-500-250.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. Higher limits cost more for the liability part of the premium.

deductible.title: Deductible
deductible.note: What you pay first on a collision or comprehensive claim. Moves only the damage share.

500.label: $500 deductible
500.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. A lower deductible raises the collision and comprehensive part of the premium.

2000.label: $2,000 deductible
2000.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. A higher deductible lowers the collision and comprehensive part of the premium.

no.label: Owned outright
no.derivation: The starting point for loan or lease.

yes.label: Loan or lease (gap coverage)
yes.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. Lenders usually require collision and comprehensive, and many drivers add gap coverage.

vehicle-age.title: Vehicle age
vehicle-age.note: Years since the model year, counted from 2026. Moves only the damage share.

0-3.label: Vehicle 0–3 years old
0-3.derivation: The starting point for vehicle age.

4-7.label: Vehicle 4–7 years old
4-7.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. Older cars are worth less, so collision and comprehensive cost less.

8-12.label: Vehicle 8–12 years old
8-12.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. Older cars are worth less, so collision and comprehensive cost less.

13-plus.label: Vehicle 13 or more years old
13-plus.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. Older cars are worth less, so collision and comprehensive cost less.

premium-split.title: How a full-coverage premium splits
premium-split.note: Shares, not multipliers. Vehicle, limit, and deductible factors only move their own share.

liability.label: Liability share of a full-coverage premium
liability.derivation: NAIC 2023 countrywide average liability premium $736.65 ÷ combined average premium (liability + collision + comprehensive) $1438.60 = 51.2%. Source: NAIC, 2022/2023 Auto Insurance Database Report, 2023 data (the same figures as data/state-baselines). For comparison, ISO's 2024 claim costs give 55.3%. Rough because it's an average across all insured cars and states. The low and high edges are our estimate; help wanted.

collision-in-physical.label: Collision share of collision + comprehensive
collision-in-physical.derivation: ISO 2024 paid-claim frequency × severity, as published by the Insurance Information Institute: bodily injury 226.22, property damage 169.25, collision 228.34, comprehensive 91.09 dollars per car-year. Collision ÷ (collision + comprehensive). Used to weight HLDI's collision and comprehensive results for a vehicle.

bodily-injury-in-liability.label: Bodily-injury share of liability
bodily-injury-in-liability.derivation: ISO 2024 paid-claim frequency × severity, as published by the Insurance Information Institute: bodily injury 226.22, property damage 169.25, collision 228.34, comprehensive 91.09 dollars per car-year. Bodily injury ÷ (bodily injury + property damage). Used to weight HLDI's bodily-injury and property-damage results for a vehicle.

range.title: How wide the range is
range.note: Not multipliers. Each one says how much less or more a real price could be when that thing changes.

typical-start.label: Starting from a typical price instead of your own
typical-start.derivation: How far companies' prices sit from the middle company for the same driver, car, and place: each premium ÷ the median premium for that profile and place (groups of 5 or more companies). Oklahoma 2026, North Dakota 2026, Texas 2025, California 2026, and Colorado 2023; median of the five states' 25th and 75th percentiles; 17746 premiums.

vehicle-model.label: How closely real prices follow our vehicle factors
vehicle-model.derivation: How far California's real prices sit from our calibrated vehicle factors, for the 11 cars in the fit: the lowest and highest of real ÷ model (each car ÷ the Accord).

vehicle-value.label: Luxury and electric cars: price can be higher still
vehicle-value.derivation: Our factors can miss high for expensive cars, because we have no public price list. When each luxury car in the calibration is left out and predicted from the others, the largest miss is real ÷ model = 1.28 (Tesla Model 3 0.82; BMW 340i 0.85; Tesla Model S 1.28; BMW 530i 1.09). Used to widen the range upward for luxury makes and electric cars.

vehicle-model-years.label: Model year outside HLDI's years
vehicle-model-years.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. HLDI's results are for 2022–24 models; an older or newer design may differ.

vehicle-mixed-powertrain.label: One trim name sold as gas and as hybrid
vehicle-mixed-powertrain.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. FuelEconomy.gov lists some trim names (for example the 2024 Honda CR-V FWD) with both gas and hybrid versions. We price the gas one unless the name says hybrid, and widen the range because yours could be either.

vehicle-luxury-class.label: Using a luxury class average instead of the exact model
vehicle-luxury-class.derivation: How far the HLDI luxury and sports-car series we keep sit from their class average, full-coverage weighting: 25th and 75th percentiles over 209 series.

vehicle-class.label: Using a class average instead of the exact model
vehicle-class.derivation: How far the HLDI series we keep sit from their class average, full-coverage weighting: 25th and 75th percentiles over 315 series.

vehicle-unknown.label: Vehicle not recognized
vehicle-unknown.derivation: How far the HLDI series we keep sit from the all-vehicle average (100), full-coverage weighting: 25th and 75th percentiles over 361 series.

vehicle-unknown-luxury.label: Luxury or sports vehicle not recognized
vehicle-unknown-luxury.derivation: How far the HLDI luxury and sports-car series we keep sit from the all-vehicle average (100), full-coverage weighting: 25th and 75th percentiles over 104 series. Used for a luxury make when we can't tell what kind of vehicle it is.

trim-limited.label: Car version only partly matched
trim-limited.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. We are not sure which version of the car it is.

trim-unresolved.label: Car version not found
trim-unresolved.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. We could not find which version of the car it is.

state-unknown.label: Moving to a state without a typical price
state-unknown.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. Average prices differ a lot between states.

state-typical.label: Moving between states with typical prices
state-typical.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. A state's typical price moves differently for different drivers.

vehicle.note: HLDI insurance losses for 2022–24 models, 100 = the average vehicle. Collision and comprehensive move only the damage share of the premium, in full. Property-damage and bodily-injury liability move only the liability share, and only partly (see the liability weight). When we don't have the exact model, we use the class average.

liabilityWeight.label: How much of a vehicle's liability losses we pass on
liabilityWeight.derivation: Our estimate, and our judgment; help wanted. Frozen at 0.52 on 22 September 2026 so that adding vehicles can't move it silently. It was chosen as the largest share of HLDI's liability results that keeps the middle 90% of the vehicles we kept then inside ISO's liability symbol band (surcharges up to 25 percent, discounts up to 20 percent, as reported by Insurance Journal in 2004). The derivation recomputes that check every build and reports it next to this value. We looked for a public insurer liability symbol table (SERFF filings, the Massachusetts residual market manual) and didn't find one; Massachusetts' vehicle rating groups apply to physical damage only. Liability factor = 1 + 0.52 × (HLDI − 1), kept inside +25% and 20% less. This build's check: the middle 90% of the 361 HLDI liability results we keep run from 42% less to +39%, and the largest weight that keeps them inside ISO's band is 0.48.

exponent.label: How strongly repair losses move the damage part
exponent.derivation: Damage factor = HLDI damage result ^ 0.38. Below 1, so real prices differ between cars less than HLDI's repair losses do. California 2026 Standard single-driver profiles (full coverage, clean record, 7,600–10,000 miles, Los Angeles, Irvine, and Alturas): each car ÷ the Accord in the same profile, same company and place, median across companies. Subaru Crosstrek 0.85 (model 0.79, before 0.69); Honda Civic 0.99 (model 1.04, before 1.07); Toyota Tacoma 0.95 (model 0.89, before 0.84); Toyota Prius 1.05 (model 0.94, before 0.98); Tesla Model 3 1.21 (model 1.38, before 1.06); Ford F-150 0.88 (model 0.97, before 0.98); BMW 340i 1.50 (model 1.66, before 1.56); Toyota RAV4 0.87 (model 0.86, before 0.77); Tesla Model S 1.80 (model 1.53, before 1.39); Chevy Silverado 0.95 (model 0.99, before 0.90); BMW 530i 1.37 (model 1.30, before 0.97). California's liability share (NAIC 2023): 46.6%. Squared log error 0.307 before calibration, 0.093 after. The range is the lowest and highest exponent when each car is left out in turn. Rough: 12 cars.

typicalStart.fleetAgeNote: S&P Global Mobility: the average US car or light truck was 12.5 years old in 2023. S&P Global Mobility put the average age of US cars and light trucks at 12.5 years in 2023, which sits on the line between our 8-12 and 13-plus bands. NAIC's collision and comprehensive averages only count cars that carry those coverages, and those cars are newer than the whole fleet, so we use the 8-12 band.

cell.label: Price change since the typical price's year
cell.derivation: Rough. U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics consumer price index for motor vehicle insurance (CUUR0000SETE), 2026-08 (848.231) ÷ the 2023 average (716.004) = 1.1847. Only applied to a typical starting price, never to a price you enter. The government index is national and covers all car insurance; one state's full-coverage price may have moved a bit more or less. We widen the range by 5 points either way.
